newsitem.title: CANADA: Investors demand answers in Bre-X mystery.
newsitem.headline: Investors demand answers in Bre-X mystery.

text.p: How could so many stock analysts and mining experts have been fooled?
Investors were trying to figure out what went wrong and who to blame on Thursday after shocking revelations that Bre-X Minerals Ltd.'s Indonesian gold discovery may be a dud.
The extent to which the Busang deposit -- once trumpeted as the biggest gold discovery of the century -- might have been overstated, will not become clear for several weeks.

For many investors the most worrying aspect of the affair was how stock analysts, geologists, investment bankers, big mining companies, government officials and regulators were all quickly swept up in the euphoria over the Indonesian discovery.
Apparently they took the company's confident claims at face value without independent confirmation.
During Bre-X's spectacular stock market rise, there were few dissenting voices, despite what some market watchers now say were warning signs.

"People should have been more skeptical when the valuations were so extreme. People should have demanded access to complete and proper due diligence" on the property," Yorkton Securities mining analyst Doug Leishman said.
"Shareholders wanted to believe the good news. I think it was a function of market greed and human psychology."
Canadian securities regulators started probing the episode on Thursday and geological consultants hired by Bre-X were to begin re-testing the Busang deposit in the Indonesian jungle.
Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh said on Thursday the company was confident in Busang's reserve potential and stood behind its technical work on the property.
After Walsh's comments, which came barely 24 hours after he had admitted there was "a strong possibility" that Bre-X's exploration results had been overstated.
Its prospective partner, Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. of New Orleans said preliminary results from seven drill holes showed "insignificant amounts" of gold.
Bre-X shares resumed trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange, down C$12 to C$3.50 in panicky trading, making investors' views abundantly clear.
The Bre-X developments reverberated across Canada like a shockwave, tarnishing its mining industry and casting a pall over its stock exchanges and the broad financial community.
Bre-X had claimed previously that the Busang deposit contained 71 million ounces of gold, worth about $20 billion at current gold prices, and projected it could hold up to 200 million ounces.

Attempts to dissect what, if anything, went wrong with Bre-X's calculations will now focus on the potentially invalid samples and assays. Such analyses are used to estimate the size of a mineral deposit based on small rock tests.
Bre-X on Thursday dismissed rumors that its samples could have been tampered with.

"Sampling and assaying is a very inexact science. There is a lot of room for error. If you are extrapolating from results which themselves may not have been sufficiently tested...you are building on a house of cards," said Hugh Leggatt of Placer Dome Inc.. Placer, a gold mining company, at one time hoped to merge with Bre-X in a $5 billion deal.
Even given a margin for error in assaying, that hardly explains the huge difference between Bre-X's claim of 71 million ounces and Freeport McMoran's study showing "insignificant amounts" of gold.

Kilborn Engineering, the Vancouver company that did the original assessment of Bre-X's drilling, stood behind its estimates, but stressed that its work consisted of modeling and other studies, not drilling or sampling.

Yorkton's Leishman said Bre-X was unorthodox because it did not save part of its core samples for later inspection as most mining companies do. It also did not provide detailed assay information or allow outsiders to do their own sampling.

The signs and persistent rumors questioning Bre-X's credibility should have caused mining analysts and the big companies, such as Placer and Toronto's Barrick Gold Corp., which sought to cut a deal with Bre-X, to be more cautious, he said.
